prompt: In 120 to 180 words, explain calibration versus discrimination for probabilistic classifiers in exactly five numbered points. Include one example metric for each and finish with a one-sentence conclusion.

turns.user_message: In 120 to 180 words, explain calibration versus discrimination for probabilistic classifiers in exactly five numbered points. Include one example metric for each and finish with a one-sentence conclusion.
turns.assistant_message:
1. Calibration refers to how well a classifier’s predicted probabilities match the true likelihood of outcomes; a well-calibrated model predicts “70% chance” that occurs ~70% of the time.  
2. Discrimination measures the model’s ability to rank instances correctly — i.e., whether it assigns higher probabilities to positive cases than negative ones, regardless of absolute probability accuracy.  
3. A key metric for calibration is the Expected Calibration Error (ECE), which quantifies the average difference between predicted confidence and empirical accuracy across probability bins.  
4. A key metric for discrimination is the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC-ROC), which evaluates the trade-off between true positive rate and false positive rate across all classification thresholds.  
5. A model can be well-calibrated but poor at discrimination (e.g., always predicting the base rate), or highly discriminative but miscalibrated (e.g., overconfident predictions).  
Conclusion: Calibration ensures probability estimates are trustworthy, while discrimination ensures the model can meaningfully distinguish between classes.
